From Alexander onward the details strongly track Ptolemaic/Seleucid rivalries, the attempted Egyptian campaigns and Antiochus IV's treatment of Judeans. Yale's Collins describes the first Persian overview as imprecise but the Hellenistic section as detailed.
records.laterUse: The final verses (11:40–45) envision a campaign and the king's demise near the holy mountain. USCCB's critical notes say those events do not correspond to the Maccabean-era record: Antiochus IV died in the East, in Persia (often geographically called the eastern satrapies), in late 164 BCE. Alternative futurist readings relocate the end to an eschatological ruler or see typology.
records.relationship: The concentration of detailed historical matches before a mismatch near 11:40–45 is a major argument for composing the final vision during Antiochus's persecution, before knowledge of his death. Distinguish an inference about probable composition from certainty about each literary layer, and examine claims that later redaction could change the forecast.
records.evidence: Seleucid succession and Antiochus's activity are independently corroborated in Greco-Roman and Jewish sources. The discrepancy at the ending is a concrete evidentiary limitation for interpretations that demand the same near-term ruler and literal geography. Later antichrist or future-horizon readings are possible interpretive alternatives, not independently verified original referents.
records.sourceStatus: Hellenistic event matches strong; final king death setting fails a straightforward Antiochus identification
refs: John J. Collins, Yale Bible Study: Daniel 10–12

records.label: Resurrection, the sealed end, and 1,290/1,335 days
records.later: Antiochene persecution, restoration, later resurrection and apocalyptic countdowns
records.kind: End-time resurrection expectation with several non-identical duration formulas
records.original: Daniel 12:2 Hebrew וְרַבִּים מִיְּשֵׁנֵי אַדְמַת־עָפָר יָקִיצוּ ('many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth shall awaken'); 12:11–12 lists 1,290 and 1,335 days.
records.setting: Daniel 12 continues the angelic disclosure of the Antiochene crisis in chapter 11. Michael protects God's people, some dead awake to life or disgrace, and the wise receive lasting honor. The text contains one of the Hebrew Bible's clearest individual resurrection formulations, though its 'many' wording does not automatically specify universal resurrection.
records.laterUse: The book offers a 'time, times and half a time' as well as 1,290 and 1,335 days, while chapter 8 uses 2,300 evenings/mornings. USCCB suggests the different figures reflect successive calculations of a hoped-for end during the persecution. Jewish and Christian communities later developed divergent teachings of resurrection and reused the countdowns for distant end times.
records.relationship: Different denominators, daily sacrifices and editorial adjustments should be compared without silently treating them as one modern-calendar prediction. The transformation from an immediate persecution context to later universal end-of-world scenarios is a documented reception-history move.
records.evidence: The crisis and temple rededication are historically studied, but no independent evidence verifies a first-century BCE mass resurrection or precisely dated world judgment. Whether the figures represent authorial corrections or coexisting symbolic schemas is debated.
records.sourceStatus: Early resurrection teaching and competing durations verifiable; worldwide end events not corroborated
refs: Daniel 12 with USCCB notes on 1,290/1,335 days
John J. Collins, Yale Bible Study: Daniel 10–12

records.label: Not one Temple stone upon another
records.later: Roman destruction of Jerusalem's Second Temple in 70 CE
records.kind: Historically testable near-term prediction with uncertain text/speech date
records.original: Mark 13:2 Greek: οὐ μὴ ἀφεθῇ ὧδε λίθος ἐπὶ λίθον ὃς οὐ μὴ καταλυθῇ ('not a stone will be left here upon a stone that will not be torn down').
records.setting: Mark describes Jesus and his followers leaving Herod's Temple complex; the disciples admire its great stones and buildings, and Jesus announces their dismantling. Mark's composition is often dated approximately 65–75 CE, around the Jewish-Roman War and Temple destruction; a pre-70 date and historical prediction are defended by other scholars.
records.laterUse: The Roman army destroyed and burned the Jerusalem Temple sanctuary in 70 CE, as historically recorded in Josephus and other sources. Substantial platform and retaining-wall masonry remains, so whether 'no stone upon another' is literal total removal or rhetorical language focused on the sacred buildings matters.
records.relationship: A report about Jesus' speech decades before the event survives in a Gospel whose final literary date relative to 70 CE is debated. A historically verified Temple destruction therefore does not independently show that this precise wording was spoken before it happened.
records.evidence: The destruction of the Temple in 70 CE is strongly evidenced, while exact independent confirmation of the speech or an earlier dated manuscript is unavailable. Remaining retaining-wall courses are distinguishable from sanctuary buildings; neither a facile literal-success claim nor a simple all-stones-standing objection accounts for that distinction.
records.sourceStatus: Temple destruction historically confirmed; literal scope and timing of recorded prediction debated
refs: S. G. F. Brandon, 'The Date of the Markan Gospel', New Testament Studies
The Synoptic Gospels, BYU Religious Studies Center — pre/post 70 dating debate

records.label: This generation will not pass until all these things happen
records.later: The first-century generation, 70 CE destruction, and still-future Son of Man expectations
records.kind: Explicit near-audience time constraint with disputed scope
records.original: Mark 13:30: ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ μέχρις οὗ ταῦτα πάντα γένηται ('this generation certainly will not pass away until all these things occur').
records.setting: Mark 13 begins with the Temple prediction, then narrates war, crisis, celestial signs and the Son of Man appearing on clouds (13:24–27). The phrase 'this generation' in Mark elsewhere usually addresses the narrative generation. Verse 32 also says no one knows the day or hour, generating an internal tension discussed by scholars.
records.laterUse: Jerusalem's Temple was destroyed in 70 CE within approximately four decades of Jesus' ministry, but there is no independent historical verification of the combined cosmic and visible Son of Man events. Christian solutions distinguish Temple-judgment from final return, treat heavenly imagery symbolically, refer to a future signs-witnessing generation or understand the noun as a spiritual kind; these readings are contested.
records.relationship: The verdict depends on precisely what 'all these things' covers. A reading referring to Jesus' contemporaries and the whole sequence through the cosmic return faces an unfulfilled deadline; restricting the horizon to the Temple's fall or redefining generation changes the claim being evaluated. Matthew and Luke's redactions require separate attention before collapsing all Synoptics.
records.evidence: Benjamin Edsall (2025) studies generation language across the Gospel tradition and its ambiguities; Scott Charlesworth (2017) finds Matthew's immediate sequence from Jerusalem's fall to cosmic signs difficult to separate; preterist and alternative critiques are active scholarship. No historical evidence establishes a visible celestial coming within the contemporaries' lifespan.
records.sourceStatus: Original time phrase explicit; 70 CE Temple event secure; all-things scope and promised return debated
refs: Benjamin A. Edsall (2025), 'This Generation' from Mark to Judas, JSNT
Scott Charlesworth (2017), Historicist interpretation of the Olivet Discourse

records.label: Before you finish Israel's towns, the Son of Man will come
records.later: The disciples' Israel mission, resurrection/exaltation interpretations, Jerusalem 70 CE and final coming
records.kind: Mission timetable and the Son of Man coming with disputed referent
records.original: Matthew 10:23: οὐ μὴ τελέσητε τὰς πόλεις τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ ἕως ἔλθῃ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('you certainly will not complete the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes').
records.setting: In a mission speech addressed to the Twelve, Matthew instructs them to preach to Israel and warns of persecutions, synagogues and rulers. The Greek passage includes a strong negative with an 'until' clause and has textual variants regarding 'of Israel' in some manuscripts. Matthew 24:14 places global mission before the end; reconciling the passages has a substantial interpretive history.
records.laterUse: Some historians see an imminent return expected during the disciples' lifetime, now historically unfulfilled. Some Christian theologians connect 'coming' to resurrection/exaltation, divine judgment on Jerusalem in 70 CE or a more distant final return. Torsten Löfstedt (2025 volume, online 2026) argues Matthew's 'coming' here is Jesus' exaltation at his resurrection, distinct from the final end.
records.relationship: The near deadline is plain, while 'coming' has competing referents. Each referent changes the event used to test fulfillment. The text itself does not state one universal calendar deadline or specify that every ancient village had to hear a fully completed modern missionary campaign.
records.evidence: Matthew's wording and historical chronology of Jesus' ministry, crucifixion and later Jerusalem fall are available for comparison. There is no independent evidence that the Son of Man visibly returned by the time the original group died. An exaltation claim can be a theological interpretation rather than an externally verifiable dated event.
records.sourceStatus: Temporal syntax and original audience clear; event meant by 'comes' disputed
refs: Torsten Löfstedt, 'The Coming of the Son of Man and the Mission to Israel'

records.label: Some standing here will not taste death before the Kingdom comes
records.later: The Transfiguration, resurrection/exaltation, Pentecost, 70 CE or future return
records.kind: Prediction within a listener's lifespan with disputed event definition
records.original: Mark 9:1 Greek: οὐ μὴ γεύσωνται θανάτου ἕως ἂν ἴδωσιν τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐληλυθυῖαν ἐν δυνάμει ('will certainly not taste death until they see God's kingdom come in power').
records.setting: Mark's declaration follows a teaching about the Son of Man coming in glory (8:38) and is immediately followed by the Transfiguration involving three disciples 'after six days' (9:2). Matthew revises the wording to the Son of Man 'coming in his kingdom'; Luke describes seeing the kingdom of God.
records.laterUse: Interpreters variously point to the Transfiguration, Jesus' resurrection and exaltation, Pentecost, Jerusalem's fall, or the final parousia. The Transfiguration is narratively close but visible only as a literary account; resurrection/exaltation is likewise claimed within Christian sources. A full final cosmic advent during those hearers' lives is not independently observed.
records.relationship: The wording sets a lifespan constraint, but readers disagree whether the promised 'coming in power' is an anticipatory vision or an ultimate eschatological transformation. Taking the verse to guarantee a final return within the listeners' lifespan confronts nonfulfillment; selecting a different event must be defended with the adjacent narrative and wider Gospel sequence.
records.evidence: NET translator notes explicitly catalog Transfiguration, resurrection, Spirit and second coming readings. E. J. Davila (New Testament Studies, 2026), writing on Mark 16:1–8, argues that Mark presents Jesus' resurrection as the beginning of the kingdom, which supports a resurrection reading of 9:1, showing that this reading is an argued alternative, not an uncontested definition.
records.sourceStatus: Lifespan language unambiguous; kingdom-arrival referent and historical verification disputed
refs: NET Bible on Mark 9:1 and four proposed fulfillments
E. J. Davila (2026), Does Mark Care That Jesus Was Raised from the Dead?, New Testament Studies

records.label: You will see the Son of Man at God's right hand and on clouds
records.later: Jesus' exaltation, judgment on Jerusalem, and claimed final coming
records.kind: Direct second-person address joined to Danielic and Davidic enthronement imagery
records.original: Mark 14:62 Greek: ὄψεσθε τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ... ἐκ δεξιῶν καθήμενον ... καὶ ἐρχόμενον μετὰ τῶν νεφελῶν ('you will see the Son of Man ... seated at the right hand ... and coming with clouds').
records.setting: At the hearing before the high priest, Mark portrays Jesus affirming his identity and combining Psalm 110's right-hand enthronement with Daniel 7's figure approaching the heavenly Ancient of Days. The second-person plural 'you will see' is heard by the priestly group and narratively implicates that audience.
records.laterUse: Some interpreters understand a near vindication shown through Jesus' resurrection, Church growth or Jerusalem's destruction; others see the final visible parousia. Matthew 26:64 adds 'from now on,' suggesting an inaugurated heavenly vindication. Murray J. Smith and Ian J. Vaillancourt (2022) explicitly argue Mark includes *both* enthronement and later future advent.
records.relationship: In Daniel 7 the humanlike figure comes toward God's throne to receive authority, a directional fact easily lost when imagining a descent to earth. A future returning Jesus is a later theological application requiring interpretation of Mark's juxtaposition and the direct audience 'you'.
records.evidence: The quoted links to Daniel and Psalm 110 are independently readable. No outside historical record verifies that the high priestly audience saw Jesus seated in heaven or on clouds. The time horizon and whether the 'seeing' is figurative judgment or literal visibility remain disputed.
records.sourceStatus: Combined sources and direct audience established; future versus inaugurated interpretation and fulfillment disputed
refs: Smith and Vaillancourt, JBL 2022, Enthroned and Coming to Reign

records.label: We the living who remain until the Lord's coming
records.later: The lifespans of Paul and his audience; Christian expectation of Jesus' return
records.kind: Early Pauline apocalypse with disputed grammatical commitment to imminent lifetime fulfillment
records.original: 1 Thessalonians 4:15 Greek ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες οἱ περιλειπόμενοι εἰς τὴν παρουσίαν τοῦ κυρίου ('we the living, the remaining, until/for the coming of the Lord').
records.setting: Paul addresses a Thessalonian Christian community concerned that people have died before Jesus' coming. The letter is commonly placed around 50–51 CE, one of the earliest extant Christian writings. It reassures readers that the dead in Christ will rise before the surviving believers join them.
records.laterUse: Paul writes in the first-person plural 'we who are alive,' which many scholars understand as his expectation that he or members of his contemporary audience could survive until an imminent return. The apostle died and no publicly verifiable descent with the trumpet, resurrection and airborne assembly took place during that generation.
records.relationship: The 'we' may be inclusive pastoral identification with the class of believers still alive *whenever* the parousia occurs rather than a categorical statement that Paul himself would survive; the Greek participle modifies this class. A 2024 Novum Testamentum article argues the imminent/near-expectation reading is only one of several grammatically defensible options. Do not assert a hard dated prophecy if the passage does not specify an explicit year.
records.evidence: The first-century letter's grammar and Paul's eventual death are historically grounded; heavenly trumpet, clouds and resurrection are not independently corroborated. Distinguish probable near expectation from an unambiguous personal survival guarantee.
records.sourceStatus: First-person and resurrection sequence explicit; guaranteed lifetime deadline contested
refs: Novum Testamentum (2024), Is There Imminent Expectation in 1 Thess 4:13–18?

records.label: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed
records.later: Paul's audience and later Christian resurrection expectations
records.kind: Pauline time expectation with exceptional Greek manuscript variants
records.original: Common critically preferred Greek: πάντες οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα ('we will not all sleep, but we will all be changed'); some manuscripts instead read 'we all will sleep, but not all will be changed'.
records.setting: In a letter commonly dated about 53–55 CE, Paul argues for resurrection and a final transformation at the last trumpet. 'Sleep' functions as a death metaphor; Paul specifies that believers' bodies must be transformed for immortality. The transmission history of verse 51 includes several markedly divergent Greek forms.
records.laterUse: In the preferred modern critical reading, Paul speaks as though some believers will remain alive at the last trumpet; later scribes transmitted alternate formulations that change the apparent lifetime expectation. No independently observable global trumpet/resurrection is established as occurring in Paul's generation.
records.relationship: Because some variants reverse key negatives, an evidence audit must name its textual base before treating the verse as a fixed expired promise. NET's textual note groups four principal variants and explains how embarrassment about Paul's generation dying could have motivated some scribal changes, without proving the motives of each copyist.
records.evidence: The critical text and manuscript variants are ascertainable; a resurrection event is not historically independently confirmable. The preferred text establishes Paul's anticipation that some living believers might be changed, but an exact year or definitive guarantee about Paul individually is absent.
records.sourceStatus: Preferred textual form and major variants documented; eschatological timeframe and miraculous event unverified
refs: Scholarly citation of Fee and Metzger on 1 Cor 15:51 variant readings

records.label: What must happen soon: the appointed time is near
records.later: Seven churches in Roman Asia; successive centuries of Christian expectations
records.kind: Explicit imminent apocalyptic framing with disputed referent and time horizon
records.original: Greek ἐν τάχει (en tachei, 'soon/quickly', Rev 1:1; 22:6), ἐγγύς (engys, 'near', 1:3; 22:10), and ἔρχομαι ταχύ ('I am coming soon/quickly', 22:7, 12, 20).
records.setting: The book introduces itself as a revelation addressed to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia. Its prologue and epilogue frame visions of imperial evil, judgment and new creation with repeated imminence language. The book's final form is commonly placed near Domitian's late-first-century reign, though early Nero-era dating and redaction models remain disputed.
records.laterUse: Christians have applied the passages to first-century divine judgment on Rome or Jerusalem, the quickly unfolding consequences of Christ's resurrection, the end-of-age return still awaited, or the claim that events happen rapidly once initiated. Readings that postpone the promised culmination indefinitely must explain both ἐν τάχει and ἐγγύς and the addressees' context.
records.relationship: A claim about soon/near events, stated to the author's contemporary readers, intersects the entire vision but does not itself specify a calendar date. 'Swiftly when it happens' can be argued for ταχύ in certain contexts, but it does not automatically cancel the explicitly spatial-temporal 'near' at both bookends. Apocalyptic symbols and stages can carry multiple referents; specify which events have occurred before rating fulfillment.
records.evidence: The original Greek expressions and named Asian congregations are directly ascertainable. No independently observed end of death, new creation, or universal visible return is documented within that audience's lifespan. Claims that the language refers only to contemporary Roman tribulation, rather than the book's cosmic end, remain interpretive positions that require argument.

records.label: The beast, coercive worship and 666/616
records.later: First-century Roman imperial institutions and subsequent end-time beast interpretations
records.kind: Apocalyptic political symbol and cryptographic number with significant textual variant
records.original: Rev 13:18 Greek ψήφισάτω τὸν ἀριθμὸν τοῦ θηρίου ('let them calculate the beast's number'); principal number ἑξακόσιοι ἑξήκοντα ἕξ (666), with ancient 616 variant.
records.setting: Revelation's sea beast borrows features from Daniel 7's four political beasts, while a land beast promotes worship of the first. In a Roman-Asia setting, imperial authority, emperor worship and restrictions on economic activity provide a historically grounded interpretive backdrop. The seven heads can be associated with Rome's rulers/hills, but the details are not straightforward chronological data.
records.laterUse: A major scholarly identification reads 666 as 'Neron Caesar' transliterated into Hebrew letters, yielding 666, with a Latinized name spelling yielding 616. Papyrus 115 preserves a form of the 616 variant; it is not a modern numerical invention. Max Nelson (2025) challenges the dominant Nero proposal with a Claudian-house candidate, confirming continuing scholarly disagreement. Many Christian futurist traditions interpret the beast as a still-future political ruler or system.
records.relationship: The number is a feature of first-century name-number calculation (gematria/isopsephy) and has manuscript variation that must be recorded before modern identifications. The text invokes Danielic empire imagery, not a directly demonstrable future identification from a present-day technology, ID system or political figure. Rome-centered readings are historically contextual but not proof that every apocalyptic image was fulfilled by Nero.
records.evidence: Roman imperial rule, Nero's death in 68 CE, Asian provincial imperial cults, and textual witnesses to 666/616 are historically documented. The chapter's supernatural miracles, global control and final downfall are not independently verified as an integrated literal event; scholars dispute single-name decoding and the intended audience/dating.
records.sourceStatus: Roman imperial context and 666/616 variants supported; beast identity and any full predictive fulfillment disputed

records.label: Thousand-year reign, final judgment and new Jerusalem
records.later: Jewish restoration imagery, Christian premillennial/amillennial/postmillennial expectations, claimed end of death
records.kind: Eschatological vision reusing older restoration images; duration and sequence contested
records.original: Rev 20:2 χίλια ἔτη ('a thousand years'); Rev 21:1 οὐρανὸν καινὸν καὶ γῆν καινήν ('new heaven and new earth'); Rev 21:4 θάνατος οὐκ ἔσται ἔτι ('death will be no more').
records.setting: A vision following the beast's judgment depicts Satan bound for one thousand years, martyrs reigning, a later release and final battle, judgment of the dead, and a new heaven and new earth descending with a vast cubic Jerusalem. The author reworks Isaiah 25, 65–66, Ezekiel 37–48 and Danielic resurrection/court imagery. The 'new city' has no separate temple because God and the Lamb embody its sanctuary.
records.laterUse: Premillennialists read a future distinct thousand-year reign followed by final judgment; amillennialists understand the thousand years symbolically as Christ's present reign with a final consummation; postmillennial readings view an extended gospel transformation before final return. Jewish and Christian readings of Isaiah/Ezekiel antecedents differ. Catholic USCCB notes explicitly interpret the millennium as a symbolic, rather than literal, long period.
records.relationship: The gigantic cube, innumerable architectural jewels and replacement of sun/temple are structured symbols; a blanket assertion that the material describes exactly 1,000 elapsed modern years is a tradition-specific premise. The promise of no more death is a more direct observable end-state condition, and no historical period has fulfilled it as a universal physical fact.
records.evidence: Earlier intertexts and competing reception histories can be verified. No independently observable global resurrection, permanent ending of death, destruction of the cosmos or descent of a jewel-built heavenly metropolis has been recorded. A future expectation is logically different from an already verified historical event.
records.sourceStatus: Apocalyptic intertexts and competing millennium interpretations attested; final world transformation unverified

records.label: Isaiah is named over a three-passage composite quotation
records.later: Mark 1:2–3, applied to John the Baptist's ministry
records.kind: Composite literary quotation with 'Isaiah' vs 'prophets' textual variant
records.original: Mark 1:2 ἐν τῷ Ἠσαΐᾳ τῷ προφήτῃ ('in Isaiah the prophet') in the early critical witnesses; later variant ἐν τοῖς προφήταις ('in the prophets'). Mark's first quoted messenger wording echoes Exodus 23:20 and Malachi 3:1; 1:3 cites Isaiah 40:3.
records.setting: Exodus's messenger originally guides Israel toward the land; Malachi warns of coming purification and a messenger before YHWH's arrival; Isaiah 40 announces comfort and a wilderness highway for YHWH during exile/restoration. None originally names John the Baptist.
records.laterUse: Mark makes John the Baptist the preparing wilderness messenger for Jesus and captions both source fragments with Isaiah. Matthew and Luke rework these traditions in their own order. Many manuscripts read 'in the prophets,' a possible smoothing of the difficult naming issue; the older/widely attested critical reading favors Isaiah.
records.relationship: Mark's introductory quotation is conflated from at least two different prophet texts and language echoed from Exodus. It is not a single uncontested exact forward-looking prediction. Attribution to the leading prophet can be an ancient composition convention; a mistaken attribution or later editorial correction are alternative scholarly explanations, but each must explain the manuscript evidence.
records.evidence: Direct primary comparison and well-documented textual variants establish the wording change. NET critical notes specify witnesses and explain why the harder Isaiah reading has early support; this determines which 'attribution problem' an analyst is actually judging. The Gospel's literary reuse does not independently corroborate John the Baptist as a uniquely predicted individual.
records.sourceStatus: Three-source composite and early Isaiah attribution supported; original referents distinct from later Christian reading

records.label: Psalm 22's garment-lot lament becomes two fulfillment actions
records.kind: Poetic lament reused as a passion scene with narrative elaboration
records.original: Psalm 22:18 יְחַלְּקוּ בְגָדַי לָהֶם וְעַל־לְבוּשִׁי יַפִּילוּ גוֹרָל ('they divide my clothes among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing').
records.setting: Psalm 22 is a first-person lament by a speaker who believes he has been abandoned and exposed to humiliating violence, before a turn toward divine deliverance and praise. Its two garment expressions use synonymous poetic parallelism to depict enemies treating the sufferer as doomed; no first-century Roman soldiers are named.
records.laterUse: All four canonical passion accounts mention garments and casting lots. John alone quotes Psalm 22 directly at this exact point and distinguishes the soldiers' dividing several garments from separately casting lots for a seamless tunic; the USCCB note describes the scene as a literal division of poetic parallelism into two narrated actions.
records.relationship: The earlier lyric describes humiliation and dispossession within a prayer, while the Gospel treats it as Jesus' fulfilled scripture. Multiple Gospels may preserve shared tradition and cannot automatically be counted as four independent eyewitness confirmations; deliberate narrative shaping around scripture is a live historical-critical possibility.
records.evidence: Psalm wording and John's allocation of the two actions can be compared. There is no external material record of the soldiers' precise lottery, so the evangelist's assertion of fulfillment cannot independently establish that every physical detail occurred as narrated.
records.sourceStatus: Scriptural quotation and parallelism clear; specific allocation scene lacks independent attestation

records.label: The Ethiopian official asks who Isaiah's suffering servant is
records.kind: Ancient Greek servant quotation used as a Christian teaching interpretation
records.original: Acts 8:33 quotes Greek ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει ἡ κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἤρθη ('in his humiliation his justice/judgment was taken away'); Hebrew Isaiah 53:8 reads מֵעֹצֶר וּמִמִּשְׁפָּט לֻקָּח ('by/from oppression and judgment he was taken').
records.setting: Isaiah's servant poem appears in Isaiah 52:13–53:12 and has disputed identity, including collective Israel, representative individual and other proposals; Isaiah 49:3 can call the servant Israel even as 49:5 depicts a mission to restore Israel. The Hebrew and ancient Greek forms of 53:8 differ significantly in their portrayal of oppression and judgment.
records.laterUse: Acts narrates a royal official of the Candace, queen of the Ethiopians (the kingdom of Kush/Meroë in Nubia), returning from worship in Jerusalem while reading Isaiah's Greek form. He asks Philip whom the prophet means, and Philip teaches that Jesus is the referent, after which the official is baptized. The narrative's question records that the passage's identity was not treated as self-evident.
records.relationship: Acts quotes the old Greek more closely than the Hebrew on the 'humiliation/justice' clause and applies an earlier servant poem to Jesus. The later interpretation is clearly documented as a claim by Acts' author and characters; it does not independently establish the earlier writer's intended identity or the historicity of the encounter.
records.evidence: USCCB's critical Acts 8 note identifies the quoted verses and evangelization role, and a direct comparison shows Hebrew/Greek wording differences. The reported angelic instructions, sudden disappearance and precise dialogue are only attested within Acts, not confirmed by independent contemporary records.
records.sourceStatus: Greek quotation and Jesus application explicit; Hebrew/Greek differences and earlier servant identity remain contested
